# Class 7: not everyone shares a slope

> **A note on the data.** Same file as Class 6: the repeated body-size measurements on the
> Lundy sparrows, keeping the rows that have both a wing and a mass. Class 6 used tarsus as
> the predictor and freed the intercept. Today the predictor is mass, the column that changes
> between one capture of a bird and the next, and we free the slope.

---

## Objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

1. Say what a random slope frees, and check *before you fit it* whether your covariate varies enough **within** groups for the question to have an answer.
2. Split a repeated-measures covariate into its within and between parts, say what one coefficient on the unsplit covariate blends, and why this comes *before* the random slope.
3. Fit `(1 + x | group)` on the within part and read σ_0, σ_1 and ρ out of the covariance block.
4. Explain why ρ changes, and can change sign, when you move the origin of the covariate without changing the model.
5. Compare the two models with AIC and a likelihood-ratio test, and say why the usual reference distribution is wrong when the thing tested is a variance.
6. Say what shrinkage does to a group's *slope*, and why three measurements keep only a little of the slope they suggest.

---

## The class

**Itchy's office, 9:00 am. TOTO has come straight from Class 6 with the caterpillar plot still open. MOMO is here early with a question she wrote down last week and did not ask. EDDIE is here. JARO is in the corridor.**

**Itchy:** Last week I drew you a picture and said one sentence about it that I want back before we start. Toto. The picture with all the bird lines in it.

**Toto:** They were all parallel.

**Itchy:** All parallel. Every bird got to sit high or low; none of them got its own steepness. Today we take that restriction out. But not the way you are about to.

**Momo:** Meaning we do not just type it.

**Itchy:** Meaning we do not just type it. A random slope asks whether the relationship between *y* and *x* differs from group to group. Before you can ask that, *x* has to differ within a group; otherwise there is nothing for a per-bird slope to be estimated *from*, and the software finds that out about ninety seconds after you do, in a worse mood. So: file first.

### Which column actually moves within a bird

```{julia}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
include("../tools/figures.jl")
using DRM, DataFrames, CSV, Statistics, Random, LinearAlgebra, Printf, CairoMakie
using Distributions: Chisq, ccdf
set_theme!(theme_itchy(:light))

raw = CSV.read("../data/2012/BodySize.csv", DataFrame; missingstring = "NA")

# Class 6's cleaning, with wing and weight the columns kept complete.
sparrows = dropmissing(raw, [:Wing, :Weight])
w_bar = mean(sparrows.Weight)
sparrows.wc = sparrows.Weight .- w_bar     # mass, centred on its own mean

# Each bird's own mean mass, and each capture's departure from it.
bird_mass = combine(groupby(sparrows, :BirdID), :Weight => mean => :m)
joined = leftjoin(sparrows, bird_mass, on = :BirdID)
sparrows.wbar = joined.m .- w_bar          # the bird's own average mass, centred
sparrows.wdev = sparrows.Weight .- joined.m   # this capture, relative to that bird

mkpath("../data/ch7")
CSV.write("../data/ch7/sparrows-weight.csv", sparrows)

n = nrow(sparrows)
bird_ids = sort(unique(sparrows.BirdID))
birds = length(bird_ids)
gi = indexin(sparrows.BirdID, bird_ids)    # each row's bird, as a position in bird_ids
nothing
```

**Itchy:** The file, cleaned as Class 6 cleaned it, with mass rather than tarsus the column kept complete. Three new things in the cell. `leftjoin(sparrows, bird_mass, on = :BirdID)` attaches each bird's mean mass to every one of its rows, matching on the identifier: a **join** does what Class 6's `Dict` did by hand. `indexin(a, b)` gives each element of `a` its position in `b`, the other lookup Class 6 built by hand. And the cell ends with `nothing`, which stops it printing a whole data frame.

```{julia}
#| label: counts
@printf("rows %d on %d birds\n\n", n, birds)

per_bird = combine(groupby(sparrows, :BirdID), nrow => :k)
for k in sort(unique(per_bird.k))
    @printf("%3d birds measured %d times\n", count(==(k), per_bird.k), k)
end
k_med = median(per_bird.k)
@printf("\nmedian measurements per bird: %.1f\n", k_med)
```

**Momo:** Two, three or four. That is not a lot of points to fit a line through.

**Itchy:** It is not, and hold that thought until the caterpillar, where it becomes the whole lesson. First: which of these columns moves *within* a bird? You have the tool. A repeatability is the share of variance that sits **between** individuals, so one minus it is the share within. The cell loops over five columns and stores what it finds in two lookup tables: `Dict{Symbol,Float64}()` is an empty `Dict` that will hold a number under each column's name, filled by `share_within[c] = ...`. `Float64.(...)` converts a column to plain decimals. And inside `combine`, `:y => (v -> ...) => :sw` is Class 1's double arrow with an anonymous function in the middle, here returning `missing` for a bird measured once, which `skipmissing` then steps over.

```{julia}
#| label: within-bird
candidates = [:Tarsus, :BillL, :BillW, :Tail, :Weight]
share_within = Dict{Symbol,Float64}()
within_sd = Dict{Symbol,Float64}()

@printf("%-8s %6s %8s %8s %12s\n", "column", "rows", "R", "1 - R", "within SD")
for c in candidates
    d0 = dropmissing(sparrows, [c])
    d = DataFrame(BirdID = d0.BirdID, y = Float64.(d0[!, c]))
    R = repeatability(drm(bf(@formula(y ~ 1 + (1|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)).estimate
    share_within[c] = 1 - R
    g = combine(groupby(d, :BirdID),
                :y => (v -> length(v) > 1 ? std(v) : missing) => :sw)
    within_sd[c] = mean(skipmissing(g.sw))
    @printf("%-8s %6d %8.4f %8.4f %12.4f\n",
            c, nrow(d), R, 1 - R, within_sd[c])
end
```

**Toto:** Tarsus is nearly all between.

**Itchy:** Tarsus is `{julia} string(round(100 * share_within[:Tarsus], digits = 1), "%")` within a bird and the rest between, which is Class 6's number arriving as a warning: a per-bird slope *on tarsus* asks `{julia} birds` birds for the steepness of a line through points stacked on top of each other. Mass is near the other end of the table: `{julia} string(round(100 * share_within[:Weight], digits = 1), "%")` of the variation in mass is a bird differing from itself.

**Eddie:** Because mass is condition and tarsus is architecture.

**Itchy:** And that distinction is worth more than today's arithmetic.

**Momo:** Then why mass? Bill width has the largest within-bird share in the table.

**Itchy:** It is, and I am glad you read the whole column, because that is the trap in this table. **A share does not tell you what the variation is made of.** A grown sparrow's bill width is architecture too; its within-bird share is large because the trait is a couple of millimetres wide and the calipers are not that precise, so most of what moves between captures is the measuring. Bill width moves `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * share_within[:BillW]), "%")` of its variation within a bird, and that movement is `{julia} round(within_sd[:BillW], digits = 4)` of a millimetre. Mass genuinely changes: a sparrow is heavier after a good week and lighter after a bad one, and `{julia} round(within_sd[:Weight], digits = 3)` grams of within-bird movement is a bird, not a ruler.

**Momo:** So the rule is not "pick the biggest share".

**Itchy:** The rule is: **pick a covariate whose within-group variation is a thing that happens, not a thing you did**, then check that its share is large enough to estimate from. Mass passes both. So today's question is: when a bird is heavier, is its wing measured longer, and **by the same amount in every bird**? Look before you model.

::: {#fig-spaghetti-data}

```{julia}
repeat_ids = sort(per_bird.BirdID[per_bird.k .>= 3])

# Every thirteenth bird in the ordering by mean mass: a rule, not a preference.
mean_mass = [mean(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== b]) for b in repeat_ids]
shown = repeat_ids[sortperm(mean_mass)][1:13:length(repeat_ids)]
cols = Makie.wong_colors()

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "mass (g)", ylabel = "wing (mm)",
    title = "$(length(shown)) birds, each caught at least three times")
scatter!(ax, sparrows.Weight, sparrows.Wing; markersize = 4, color = (:grey, 0.3))
for (i, b) in enumerate(shown)
    d = sort(sparrows[sparrows.BirdID .== b, :], :Weight)
    scatter!(ax, d.Weight, d.Wing; markersize = 10, color = cols[i])
    lines!(ax, d.Weight, d.Wing; color = (cols[i], 0.7), linewidth = 1.4)
end
fig
```

Every thirteenth bird in the ordering by mean mass, among those measured at least three times, its captures joined in order of mass and one colour per bird. Grey is the whole file. A random slope is the claim that these segments do not all have the same steepness.

:::

**Toto:** Some of them go up and some of them go down.

**Itchy:** And *that* is the thing we are about to put a number on. Whether the up-and-down is real or is what three points do when you join them is the content of the hour. `sort(df, :Weight)` in that cell puts a data frame's rows in order of one column; `Makie.wong_colors()` is a list of seven colours that stay distinct.

### The slope you have been sharing

**Itchy:** Two fits, in order of how much they let the birds get away with. Watch the slope and its standard error, because Class 6 left you a promise about it.

```{julia}
#| label: two-fits-wc
pooled_fit = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc)),                   Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
ri_fit     = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc + (1|BirdID))),      Gaussian(); data = sparrows)

@printf("%-16s %10s %10s %12s\n", "", "slope", "SE", "residual SD")
for (nm, f) in (("no bird at all", pooled_fit), ("+ (1|BirdID)", ri_fit))
    @printf("%-16s %10.4f %10.4f %12.4f\n",
            nm, coef(f, :mu)[2], stderror(f)[2], first(sigma(f)))
end
b_pooled, se_pooled = coef(pooled_fit, :mu)[2], stderror(pooled_fit)[2]
b_ri, se_ri = coef(ri_fit, :mu)[2], stderror(ri_fit)[2]
s_pooled = first(sigma(pooled_fit));
```

**Momo:** The standard error went **down**. Last week it went up.

**Itchy:** Last week I promised you a predictor where it goes the other way. This is it. Read the third column.

**Toto:** The residual standard deviation collapsed.

**Itchy:** From `{julia} round(s_pooled, digits = 4)` millimetres to `{julia} round(first(sigma(ri_fit)), digits = 4)`, a factor of `{julia} round((s_pooled / first(sigma(ri_fit)))^2, digits = 1)` in residual *variance*. **Two things happen at once when you add `(1 | g)`**: you stop counting repeated measurements as fresh evidence, which pushes the standard error up, and you take noise out of the residual, which pulls it down. On tarsus there was almost no noise for the bird term to take out, so the first won. On mass there is a great deal, and the second wins even though mass is still `{julia} string(round(100 * (1 - share_within[:Weight]), digits = 1), "%")` between-bird: the standard error is cut by `{julia} string(round(100 * (1 - se_ri / se_pooled), digits = 1), "%")`. Keep the two mechanisms; which one wins is a fact about the file, not a rule.

**Toto:** And the slope halved.

**Itchy:** More than halved, from `{julia} round(b_pooled, digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(b_ri, digits = 4)` millimetres of wing per gram, and that is bigger than today's subject. The pooled line answers a blend of two questions — heavier birds are bigger birds, and a given bird gains and loses mass — and a bird term changes the blend without separating it. So separate it now, before we free anything; it takes one line and one parameter.

### The covariate that was two covariates

**Itchy:** Split mass into two columns: the bird's **own average mass**, a fact about the bird, and each capture's **departure from that average**, a fact about the day. The setup cell built both, `wbar` and `wdev`, and they add back up to `wc`, so nothing has been added to the data. Give them separate coefficients. The table counts parameters with `dof`, Class 5b's call: intercept, slopes, σ, and every variance the random part carries.

```{julia}
#| label: split
# wbar + wdev = wc, and the two are orthogonal by construction.
sep_ri = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
bs, ses = coef(sep_ri, :mu), stderror(sep_ri)

@printf("%-26s %7s %10s %11s\n", "", "params", "logLik", "AIC")
for (nm, f) in (("wc + (1|BirdID)", ri_fit), ("wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID)", sep_ri))
    @printf("%-26s %7d %10.4f %11.4f\n", nm, dof(f), loglik(f), aic(f))
end

@printf("\nwithin-bird slope  : %+.4f   SE %.4f   z %5.2f\n", bs[2], ses[2], bs[2] / ses[2])
@printf("between-bird slope : %+.4f   SE %.4f   z %5.2f\n", bs[3], ses[3], bs[3] / ses[3])
@printf("unsplit, from above: %+.4f\n", b_ri)
d_aic_split = aic(ri_fit) - aic(sep_ri)
@printf("\nAIC bought by ONE extra fixed parameter: %.4f\n", d_aic_split)
```

**Toto:** The two slopes are nothing like each other.

**Itchy:** Nothing like each other. Between birds, `{julia} round(bs[3], digits = 4)` millimetres of wing per gram, with a *z* of `{julia} round(bs[3] / ses[3], digits = 1)`: bigger birds are heavier birds and have longer wings, which is not news and not a question anyone needed a random slope to ask. Within a bird, `{julia} round(bs[2], digits = 4)`, with a standard error of `{julia} round(ses[2], digits = 4)` and a *z* of `{julia} round(bs[2] / ses[2], digits = 2)`. **On this file there is no detectable within-bird effect of mass on wing at all.** And the unsplit coefficient from the last cell, `{julia} round(b_ri, digits = 4)`, sits between them, because that is what a blend does.

**Momo:** So a paper that reports the one coefficient is reporting neither.

**Itchy:** It is reading a between-bird fact and a within-bird fact through one number, the oldest mistake in the repeated-measures literature. And read the AIC: one extra fixed parameter buys `{julia} round(d_aic_split, digits = 2)`. Remember that number, because the random slope, which costs two, is about to buy less. **The cheapest thing on this page is not going to be the random slope. It is noticing that a covariate with a within part and a between part is two covariates.** It belongs in every repeated-measures model you fit.

**Eddie:** And the random slope?

**Itchy:** Now has a column to go on: a bird can only have its own slope on the column that moves within it, and that column is now in the model under its own name.

### Freeing the slope

> **μ_ij = (β0 + u_0j) + (β1 + u_1j) x_ij + β2 m_j, with (u_0j, u_1j) ~ N(0, Σ) and y_ij ~ N(μ_ij, σ²)**
>
> **Σ = [σ_0², ρ σ_0 σ_1 ; ρ σ_0 σ_1, σ_1²]**

**Itchy:** Measurement *i* on bird *j*. x_ij is `wdev`, the capture's departure from its own bird's average mass; m_j is `wbar`, that average, and β2 the between-bird slope you just read. The rest is Class 6 with two additions. u_0j is the bird's own nudge to the intercept, exactly last week's u_j. u_1j is the bird's own nudge to the **slope**, and it is new. They are drawn together, from a two-dimensional normal, so Σ holds three numbers rather than one: σ_0 the spread of intercepts, σ_1 the spread of slopes, and ρ the correlation between a bird's intercept and its slope.

**Eddie:** Three numbers, and the model gained two parameters rather than one.

**Itchy:** Two: σ_1 and ρ, and that is what the test will test. In code it is one term, and Toto has already typed it.

```{julia}
#| label: fit-uncentred
#| error: true
drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ Weight + (1 + Weight|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
```

**Toto:** That is not a warning, that is a crash.

**Itchy:** That is a crash, and it is the line most people type first. Two things are wrong with it, and only one of them crashed. The crash is the optimiser failing on a covariate whose zero sits far outside its range: the lightest bird in the file weighs `{julia} round(minimum(sparrows.Weight), digits = 1)` grams, so `Weight` puts every bird's intercept at a sparrow of no grams. That is an arithmetic failure inside the software, not a fact about the model, and the table after the next fit proves it; the post-mortem is in [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html). The cure is to centre: put zero somewhere the data are. The other thing wrong is the one we just spent ten minutes on: that line puts the per-bird slope on the blended column. Put it on the within column, which is centred already on each bird's own average, and both problems go at once.

```{julia}
#| label: fit-within
rs_fit = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1 + wdev|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
rs_fit
```

**Toto:** `wdev` in both places, and `wbar` staying in the fixed part.

**Itchy:** Same response, same family, one term more, and it converges. There is no `resd` line this time; there is a random-effect covariance block, printed in the form the optimiser works with rather than as σ_0, σ_1 and ρ. `vc(fit)` hands you Σ itself, and the next cell takes the three numbers out: `V[1, 1]` is row one, column one of a matrix, `V[1, 2]` the entry beside it.

```{julia}
#| label: read-the-block
V = vc(rs_fit)[:BirdID]                      # the 2x2 covariance of (intercept, slope)
sd0, sd1 = sqrt(V[1, 1]), sqrt(V[2, 2])
rho = V[1, 2] / (sd0 * sd1)
sigma_e = first(sigma(rs_fit))
b_rs = coef(rs_fit, :mu)                     # intercept, within slope, between slope

@printf("sigma_0 (spread of bird intercepts) : %.4f mm\n", sd0)
@printf("sigma_1 (spread of bird slopes)     : %.4f mm per g\n", sd1)
@printf("rho     (their correlation)         : %+.4f\n", rho)
@printf("sigma   (within a bird)             : %.4f mm\n\n", sigma_e)
@printf("within-bird slope beta1             : %.4f   SE %.4f\n",
        b_rs[2], stderror(rs_fit)[2])
```

**Toto:** So a bird's own slope is the within-bird slope plus its nudge, and the nudges have a standard deviation of `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)`.

**Itchy:** Compare that with the within-bird slope itself, `{julia} round(b_rs[2], digits = 4)`: the spread of the slopes is `{julia} round(sd1 / b_rs[2], digits = 1)` times the average slope, so at face value a good number of these birds lose measured wing as they put on mass, while the average bird gains a little. Whether to take it at face value is the second half of the hour. First, the proof about the crash.

### One model, written four ways

**Itchy:** Fit the same model at four origins, changing nothing else. `wdev` is zero at each bird's own average mass; move that zero five grams down, one gram down, leave it, move it five grams up. `at_origin` does one fit and ends with `return` and a NamedTuple, the explicit way of saying what a function hands back; `map(at_origin, origins)` calls it on each origin and collects the four results, a comprehension by another name.

```{julia}
#| label: origins
function at_origin(origin)
    d = DataFrame(BirdID = sparrows.BirdID, Wing = sparrows.Wing, wbar = sparrows.wbar,
                  x = sparrows.wdev .- origin)
    f = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ x + wbar + (1 + x|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)
    W = vc(f)[:BirdID]
    s0, s1 = sqrt(W[1, 1]), sqrt(W[2, 2])
    return (; sd0 = s0, sd1 = s1, rho = W[1, 2] / (s0 * s1),
            sigma = first(sigma(f)), aic = aic(f))
end

origins = [-5.0, -1.0, 0.0, 5.0]
@printf("%-14s %9s %9s %9s %9s %12s\n",
        "x = wdev -", "sigma_0", "sigma_1", "rho", "sigma", "AIC")
rows = map(at_origin, origins)
for (o, r) in zip(origins, rows)
    @printf("%-14.1f %9.4f %9.4f %+9.4f %9.5f %12.4f\n",
            o, r.sd0, r.sd1, r.rho, r.sigma, r.aic)
end
@printf("\nlargest AIC difference across the four: %.3e\n",
        maximum(r.aic for r in rows) - minimum(r.aic for r in rows))
```

**Toto:** The correlation changed sign.

**Itchy:** The correlation changed sign, from `{julia} round(rows[1].rho, digits = 4)` five grams below a bird's own average to `{julia} round(rows[end].rho, digits = 4)` five grams above it. And read the other columns before anyone gets excited: σ_1 is the same to four decimal places in every row, σ is the same, and the AIC differs by `{julia} @sprintf("%.0e", maximum(r.aic for r in rows) - minimum(r.aic for r in rows))`. **These are not four models. This is one model, written down four ways.** That is the proof about the crash: where zero sits is not part of the model, so a fit that dies when zero moves has died of arithmetic. Ten grams of shift changed nothing; the uncentred line asked for about `{julia} round(Int, w_bar)` grams, to a mass no sparrow has, and the optimiser could not get there.

**Momo:** Then what is ρ about?

**Itchy:** ρ is the correlation between a bird's slope and its intercept, and its **intercept is its predicted wing length at x equal to zero**. Move zero and you are asking about the bird's wing length at a different mass, so of course the correlation changes. Five grams below a bird's own average is lighter than that bird was ever weighed, so "intercept" there is an extrapolation backwards, and a bird with a steeper slope necessarily extrapolates lower — a negative correlation, manufactured by the arithmetic. Five grams above, the tilt goes the other way. At a bird's own average, ρ is closest to being about the birds and not the origin, and that is the origin `wdev` gives every bird for free. So: report ρ with its origin in the same sentence, and centre a covariate whose zero is outside its range, every time.

**Toto:** Show me the sign change instead of making me read it off a column.

**Itchy:** Fair — ρ is a function of one number, where you put zero, and that is a curve, not four fits. Shift the origin by *t* and each bird's intercept becomes its old intercept plus *t* times its slope, so the board's Σ moves like this, with nothing refitted:

> **u_0j' = u_0j + t u_1j, so Var(u_0') = σ_0² + 2t ρσ_0σ_1 + t²σ_1², Cov(u_0', u_1) = ρσ_0σ_1 + tσ_1², and σ_1 does not move.**

```{julia}
#| label: fig-origin-rho
#| fig-cap: "ρ as a function of where the within-bird covariate is centred, computed from the one fitted Σ by the shift on the board, with no refitting: negative below the dotted zero line and positive above it, crossing zero to the left of the shaded strip. The four diamonds are the four origins from the table, each labelled with its ρ. The shaded strip is how far any capture sits from its own bird's average mass; five grams either way is outside it, so ρ there is an extrapolation."
rho_at(t) = (V[1, 2] + t * V[2, 2]) /
            sqrt((V[1, 1] + 2t * V[1, 2] + t^2 * V[2, 2]) * V[2, 2])
t_zero = -V[1, 2] / V[2, 2]                      # where the correlation is exactly zero
t_grid = range(minimum(origins) - 1, maximum(origins) + 1, length = 200)

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "origin, in grams from the bird's own average mass",
    ylabel = "correlation ρ", title = "One curve, not four fits")
vspan!(ax, minimum(sparrows.wdev), maximum(sparrows.wdev); color = (:grey, 0.08))
hlines!(ax, [0.0]; linestyle = :dot, color = (:grey, 0.6))
lines!(ax, t_grid, rho_at.(t_grid); linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax, origins, [r.rho for r in rows]; markersize = 11, marker = :diamond)
for (t, r) in zip(origins, rows)
    text!(ax, t, r.rho; text = string(round(r.rho, digits = 2)),
        align = (:center, :bottom), offset = (0, 8), fontsize = 12)
end
fig
```

**Itchy:** ρ is exactly zero at an origin of `{julia} round(t_zero, digits = 2)` grams, outside the strip: no capture in this file is that far from its bird's average, the furthest below being `{julia} round(minimum(sparrows.wdev), digits = 2)`. And the four points are the four rows of that table, now impossible to mistake for four models.

**Momo:** Then what is the ρ we have?

**Itchy:** `{julia} round(rho, digits = 4)`, at each bird's own average mass: a bird that is longer-winged at its own average mass tends to gain more measured wing per gram it puts on. A within-bird statement, because the column it sits on is the within column. Hold it lightly all the same. This engine prints the correlation with no standard error beside it; its R twin prints both ([Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html)). Either way, ρ is estimated from `{julia} birds` birds with a median of `{julia} round(Int, k_med)` captures each, which is very little, and you will see what three rows do to it. **Fit the correlation because leaving it out constrains the model; do not build a story on it.**

### Is the extra term worth it

**Itchy:** Two models, nested, one estimator. Toto, before we test anything, the cheap comparison.

```{julia}
#| label: compare-aic
@printf("%-30s %8s %12s %12s\n", "", "params", "logLik", "AIC")
for (nm, f) in (("wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID)", sep_ri), ("wdev + wbar + (1 + wdev|BirdID)", rs_fit))
    @printf("%-30s %8d %12.4f %12.4f\n", nm, dof(f), loglik(f), aic(f))
end
d_aic = aic(sep_ri) - aic(rs_fit)
@printf("\nAIC drops by %.4f for two extra parameters\n", d_aic)
```

**Toto:** Less than the split bought.

**Itchy:** For one parameter, and AIC has already charged two for this one. It is still a drop. Now the test: the naive question first, and read what the engine says back.

```{julia}
#| label: naive-lrt
lrtest(sep_ri, rs_fit)
```

**Momo:** It gave me the number and told me not to use it.

**Itchy:** Read the warning as three sentences. The first says why the number is wrong: σ_1 cannot be negative, so testing it at zero is a test on the boundary of the parameter space, and χ² with two degrees of freedom is not the right reference. The second says which way it is wrong: too large, so the test loses power rather than inventing significance. The third names the engine's own correction, built for two *independent* variances on the boundary — not what we added, one variance and one correlation — so we will not use it; [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html) has the two mixtures side by side. Class 8 takes the boundary apart properly; today you need one fact, and Jaro is in the corridor.

**Jaro:** *(from the doorway)* You want the mixture. Self and Liang (1987) worked out what the likelihood-ratio statistic does when the null sits on the boundary of the parameter space; Stram and Lee (1994) applied it to the mixed model, for exactly the step you have just taken — *q* random effects against *q* plus one, and here *q* is one. Of the two parameters you added, the variance sits on a boundary and the correlation does not, and when the variance goes to zero the correlation stops existing at all. For that case the null is a **fifty-fifty mixture of chi-squared with one degree of freedom and chi-squared with two**. One line of arithmetic.

```{julia}
#| label: boundary-lrt
stat = 2 * (loglik(rs_fit) - loglik(sep_ri))

# Stram & Lee (1994), q = 1: a 50:50 mixture of chi-squared with 1 and 2 df.
p_sl(s) = 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(1), s) + 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(2), s)

@printf("LR statistic                                  : %.4f\n\n", stat)
@printf("naive chi-squared(2)                          : %.4f\n", ccdf(Chisq(2), stat))
@printf("Stram & Lee mixture, 0.5 chi2(1) + 0.5 chi2(2): %.4f\n", p_sl(stat))
```

**Toto:** Both under five percent.

**Itchy:** Both under five percent, neither by a mile, which is exactly when the reference distribution earns its keep: `{julia} round(ccdf(Chisq(2), stat), digits = 3)` from the naive reference, `{julia} round(p_sl(stat), digits = 3)` from the mixture. The naive one is the conservative one; the mixture is the right one for this step. **Read the assumptions on a correction before you take its p-value.**

**Momo:** And if I still do not believe σ_1? How do I know the model would not find a spread of slopes in data with none?

**Itchy:** You simulate a world with none, refit, and count how often it says otherwise — a parametric bootstrap of the test, which Class 8 builds.

### What the model does to a bird's own slope

**Eddie:** The model says the spread of slopes is `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 3)`. If I fit a line through one bird's own points, do I get its slope?

**Itchy:** You do not, and the gap is the lesson. Take the birds with at least three captures, fit each bird's own line by least squares with nothing borrowed, and put those next to what the model predicts for the same birds. `B[:, 2]` is the whole second column of a matrix; `enumerate` hands the loop each bird with its position.

```{julia}
#| label: own-slopes
B = ranef(rs_fit)[:BirdID]                 # birds x 2: column 1 intercepts, column 2 slopes
model_slope = b_rs[2] .+ B[:, 2]

ols = zeros(length(repeat_ids))            # each bird's own least-squares slope
xspread = zeros(length(repeat_ids))        # and the spread of its masses
for (i, b) in enumerate(repeat_ids)
    m = sparrows.BirdID .== b
    x, y = sparrows.wdev[m], sparrows.Wing[m]
    ols[i] = cov(x, y) / var(x)
    xspread[i] = std(sparrows.Weight[m])
end
mod = model_slope[indexin(repeat_ids, bird_ids)]

@printf("birds with at least three captures : %d of %d\n\n", length(repeat_ids), birds)
@printf("%-24s %9s %9s %9s\n", "", "SD", "min", "max")
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "each bird on its own",   std(ols), minimum(ols), maximum(ols))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "the model's slopes",     std(mod), minimum(mod), maximum(mod))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "the model, all birds",
        std(model_slope), minimum(model_slope), maximum(model_slope))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f\n", "sigma_1 from the fit", sd1)
@printf("\nSD ratio, model to own: %.4f\n", std(mod) / std(ols))

# The tightest mass spread and the most extreme own slope, found from the data.
tightest, worst = argmin(xspread), argmin(ols)
for (lab, i) in (("tightest spread", tightest), ("worst own slope", worst))
    @printf("%-16s %s: masses %s, within-bird SD %.4f, own slope %.4f\n", lab, repeat_ids[i],
            string(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== repeat_ids[i]]), xspread[i], ols[i])
end
```

**Toto:** The birds' own slopes are enormous. One of them is nearly minus six.

**Itchy:** One of them is nearly `{julia} round(minimum(ols), digits = 2)` millimetres of wing per gram, which would mean a sparrow's wing shortening by half a centimetre when it eats. It is not real, and the two printed lines name the pair that shows why. `{julia} repeat_ids[tightest]` has the tightest mass spread of any bird with three or more captures — `{julia} round(xspread[tightest], digits = 4)` grams, against the file's average of `{julia} round(within_sd[:Weight], digits = 4)` — and its own slope is `{julia} round(ols[tightest], digits = 4)`. `{julia} repeat_ids[worst]` has an almost identical spread, `{julia} round(xspread[worst], digits = 4)` grams, and its own slope is `{julia} round(ols[worst], digits = 4)`. Near-identical tiny mass spreads, one dead flat and one falling off a cliff: that is what dividing a difference in wing by a difference in mass that small buys you. Draw it.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slope-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Class 6's caterpillar, now for slopes: each bird's own least-squares slope, and what the model predicts for the same bird. Every sixth bird in the ordering by its own slope, a rule and not a preference."
sel = sortperm(ols)[1:6:length(repeat_ids)]
pos = 1:length(sel)

fig = Figure(size = (520, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xticks = (pos, repeat_ids[sel]), xticklabelrotation = π / 3, xticklabelsize = 10,
    ylabel = "slope of wing on mass (mm per g)", title = "Shrinkage, now for slopes")
for (i, j) in enumerate(sel)
    lines!(ax, [i - 0.15, i + 0.15], [ols[j], mod[j]]; color = (:grey, 0.6))
end
scatter!(ax, pos .- 0.15, ols[sel]; markersize = 8, label = "the bird's own slope")
scatter!(ax, pos .+ 0.15, mod[sel]; markersize = 8, marker = :diamond, label = "the model's slope")
Legend(fig[2, 1], ax; orientation = :horizontal, framevisible = false)
fig
```

**Eddie:** The diamonds are almost flat.

**Itchy:** The diamonds are almost flat, the circles are all over the plot, and the ratio of their spreads is `{julia} round(std(mod) / std(ols), digits = 3)`: a bird keeps about `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * std(mod) / std(ols)), "%")` of the slope its own points suggest. That is not the model being timid; it is the model observing that three points and a within-bird spread of about one gram cannot tell it much — Class 6's arithmetic, applied to a slope instead of a mean.

**Momo:** Then why is the spread of the model's slopes over all `{julia} birds` birds, `{julia} round(std(model_slope), digits = 4)`, smaller than σ_1, which is `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)`?

**Itchy:** Because a predicted effect is shrunk and a variance component is not. σ_1 is how much bird slopes *really* differ; the spread of the predictions is how much the model is willing to *say* they differ on the evidence, and the second is the smaller **in expectation**, in every mixed model you will ever fit. Quoting one as the other is a mistake people have written papers about. Now the same fit drawn as lines, the picture that names the chapter.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-bird-lines
#| fig-cap: "One population line, and one line per bird, each drawn at that bird's own average mass. In Class 6's version every line was parallel."
xs = range(minimum(sparrows.wdev), maximum(sparrows.wdev), length = 50)
wbar_of = bird_mass.m .- w_bar               # each bird's own average mass, centred, in bird order
wbar_of = wbar_of[indexin(bird_ids, bird_mass.BirdID)]

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "mass, relative to the bird's own average (g)", ylabel = "wing (mm)",
    title = "$(birds) intercepts and $(birds) slopes")
scatter!(ax, sparrows.wdev, sparrows.Wing; markersize = 4, color = (:grey, 0.3))
for j in 1:birds
    lines!(ax, xs, (b_rs[1] + b_rs[3] * wbar_of[j] + B[j, 1]) .+ (b_rs[2] + B[j, 2]) .* xs;
        color = (:grey, 0.20), linewidth = 0.6)
end
lines!(ax, xs, b_rs[1] .+ b_rs[2] .* xs; linewidth = 3)
fig
```

**Toto:** They fan out.

**Itchy:** And they cross, which parallel lines cannot do. That is the constant this class freed.

### Is the model any good

**Itchy:** Residuals, and Class 6's trap is still set: `fitted` and `residuals` on these fits are **marginal**, the population line with every bird effect set to zero, so a quantile residual comes out about twice as wide as it should (the cell's first line) — and under a random slope the width it should have depends on *x* as well, so it is not even wrong by a constant. Subtract the bird's own predicted line — both parts of it now, the intercept nudge and the slope nudge — and you have the conditional residual, which is what σ is a claim about. And before you draw anything, look for the rows a long way from their own bird, because there are some in this file and they will set the scale of the plot if you let them.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-worm
#| fig-cap: "Worm plot of the conditional residuals, standardised by a spread the flagged rows were left out of, with the rows left in the plot. A well-behaved model gives a flat line inside the band. The two points at the bottom left are the two rows the printout names as sitting below their bird; the row named as sitting above its bird ends the run leaving the band at the top right."
rq = residuals(rs_fit; type = :quantile, rng = MersenneTwister(70))
cond = sparrows.Wing .- fitted(rs_fit) .- B[gi, 1] .- B[gi, 2] .* sparrows.wdev

@printf("SD of quantile residuals    : %.4f   (it should be 1)\n", std(rq))
@printf("SD of conditional residuals : %.4f   (sigma is %.4f)\n\n", std(cond), sigma_e)

# Rows more than three residual SDs from their own bird's line, named.
bad = findall(abs.(cond ./ std(cond)) .> 3)
keep = setdiff(1:n, bad)
for i in bad
    m = sparrows.BirdID .== sparrows.BirdID[i]
    @printf("%s recorded at Wing %.1f; its own wings %s at masses %s\n",
            sparrows.BirdID[i], sparrows.Wing[i], string(sparrows.Wing[m]), string(sparrows.Weight[m]))
end
bad_below = count(cond[bad] .< 0)
@printf("\nrows flagged: %d, %d below their own bird and %d above\n",
        length(bad), bad_below, length(bad) - bad_below)

# Standardise by a spread those rows cannot set, then draw.
z = cond ./ std(cond[keep])
fig_diagnostic(z; title = "within-bird residuals, random-slope fit")
```

**Toto:** Short of σ again.

**Itchy:** Short of σ again, for Class 6's reason: each bird's two numbers were estimated from its own few rows before being subtracted, so the residual comes up short, and shrinkage, which leaves a little of each bird's effect behind, only partly offsets that. So the plot can tell you whether the within-bird wobble is symmetric, normal-ish and free of trend, and not whether σ is right. The middle of the worm is flat, which is the part the plot is for. The `{julia} length(bad)` rows the cell named are the two points at the bottom left and the end of the run at the top right; read their lines: `{julia} bad_below` are a bird recorded far below its own other captures, one a bird recorded far above. Wing in this file is a whole number in `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * mean(sparrows.Wing .== round.(sparrows.Wing))), "%")` of rows and σ is `{julia} round(sigma_e, digits = 4)` millimetres, so a dropped digit is as live a hypothesis as a broken primary. **This is a finding about the file, not about random slopes**, so Class 6's rule applies: report the fit with the rows in, and say in one sentence what moves with them out.

```{julia}
#| label: rows-out
#| warning: false
keep_ri = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID))),        Gaussian(); data = sparrows[keep, :])
keep_rs = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1 + wdev|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows[keep, :])
W3 = vc(keep_rs)[:BirdID]
rho3 = W3[1, 2] / sqrt(W3[1, 1] * W3[2, 2])

@printf("sigma,             rows in vs out : %.4f vs %.4f\n", sigma_e, first(sigma(keep_rs)))
@printf("AIC for the slope, rows in vs out : %.4f vs %.4f\n", d_aic, aic(keep_ri) - aic(keep_rs))
@printf("rho,               rows in vs out : %+.4f vs %+.4f\n", rho, rho3)
```

**Itchy:** `sparrows[keep, :]` is the rows listed in `keep` and every column. With `{julia} length(bad)` rows out of `{julia} n`, σ moves from `{julia} round(sigma_e, digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(first(sigma(keep_rs)), digits = 4)`, and the random slope's advantage in AIC shrinks from `{julia} round(d_aic, digits = 2)` to `{julia} round(aic(keep_ri) - aic(keep_rs), digits = 2)`: it survives, but it was leaning on those rows harder than the plot suggests. And the third line is the promise about ρ: without those rows it goes to `{julia} round(rho3, digits = 2)`, the edge of what a correlation can be, which says the model can no longer tell a bird's intercept nudge from its slope nudge — the birds are doing one thing, not two. The engine warns, on that fit, that standard errors at such an edge are not to be trusted; it is right. Two things you may not do: quote σ from this fit as if those rows belonged in it, and read a worm plot standardised by a spread the outliers helped to set.

### What the blended fit would have said

**Itchy:** Last thing, and it is the model most people fit: the random slope on the whole of mass, `wc`, nothing split. Fit it, and see what I would have told you if we had freed the slope first and split afterwards.

```{julia}
#| label: blended
blend_rs = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc + (1 + wc|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
sd1_blend = sqrt(vc(blend_rs)[:BirdID][2, 2])
stat_blend = 2 * (loglik(blend_rs) - loglik(ri_fit))

@printf("%-10s %9s %9s %12s\n", "", "sigma_1", "LR", "AIC bought")
@printf("%-10s %9.4f %9.4f %12.4f\n", "blended",   sd1_blend, stat_blend, aic(ri_fit) - aic(blend_rs))
@printf("%-10s %9.4f %9.4f %12.4f\n", "separated", sd1,       stat,       d_aic)
@printf("\nshare of the blended LR that was fixed-effect misspecification: %.1f%%\n",
        100 * (1 - stat / stat_blend))
```

**Toto:** σ_1 is `{julia} round(sd1_blend / sd1, digits = 1)` times as big.

**Itchy:** `{julia} round(sd1_blend, digits = 4)` against `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)`, and a likelihood-ratio statistic of `{julia} round(stat_blend, digits = 2)` against `{julia} round(stat, digits = 2)`: had I put the slope on the unsplit column, **`{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * (1 - stat / stat_blend)), "%")` of the evidence I showed you for random slopes would have been evidence for a misspecified fixed part.** The mechanism is one line of algebra: a per-bird slope on the blended column multiplies **both** parts, u_1j times the within deviation *and* u_1j times the bird's own average, so the slope variance has to absorb the between-versus-within contrast the fixed part refused to separate. It is doing two jobs. Give the fixed part its second coefficient first and σ_1 only ever has one.

**Eddie:** And the blended random slope buys `{julia} round(aic(ri_fit) - aic(blend_rs), digits = 2)` of AIC for two parameters, when the split bought `{julia} round(d_aic_split, digits = 2)` for one.

**Itchy:** **The cheapest thing on this page was never the random slope.** The finding survives the split — birds do differ in slope on this file, by `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * sd1 / sd1_blend), "%")` of what the blended model would have said, with the rows-out caveat — but what you write in a paper is the separated model's numbers, because that is the model that asks the within-bird question: AIC improves by `{julia} round(d_aic, digits = 2)` for the random slope, and the boundary-corrected p is `{julia} round(p_sl(stat), digits = 3)`. And the order is the sentence to take home: **fit the decomposition first, then ask whether the within slope varies.**

### What has to wait

**Itchy:** One note and then the summary. Everything today has been Gaussian, and the obvious next question is a random slope on a **binary** outcome — does a treatment's effect on survival differ between broods. This engine does not yet fit one ([Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html)); when it does, everything here transfers, with the standard deviations read on the log-odds scale.

**Toto:** So today's summary is: not everyone shares a slope.

**Itchy:** Not everyone shares a slope, the model will tell you how much they differ, and it will charge you two parameters and one correlation you have to interpret carefully.

## Summary

### Stats stuff

- **What a random slope frees.** `(1 + x | g)` lets each group have its own steepness as well as its own height; the group lines stop being parallel and cross.
- **Check the covariate before you fit.** A random slope needs *x* to vary **within** groups; one minus the repeatability of *x* is the share that does, and what that variation *is* matters as much as its size: bill width moves because the calipers do, mass because the bird does.
- **A coefficient on a repeated-measures covariate blends two slopes, and splitting them costs one parameter.** Here between-bird `{julia} round(bs[3], digits = 3)`, within-bird `{julia} round(bs[2], digits = 3)`, and the split bought more AIC for one parameter than the random slope for two. **Fit the decomposition first; then ask whether the within slope varies.**
- **Standard errors can go either way.** Adding `(1 | g)` stops counting repeated measurements as fresh evidence, which raises the standard error, and removes noise from the residual, which lowers it; here the second won.
- **Two parameters, not one.** A random slope adds a variance **and** a covariance, and the comparison must charge for both.
- **ρ is a statement about where zero is.** Move the origin of *x* and ρ changes, and can change sign, while the likelihood, the AIC, σ, σ_1 and the fixed slope do not move. Report ρ with the origin in the same sentence, and centre a covariate whose zero is outside its range, every time: a far-away origin can crash the optimiser without changing the model.
- **Testing σ_1 = 0 is a boundary problem.** The naive χ²(2) is conservative. Stram and Lee (1994) cover exactly this step, *q* random effects against *q* + 1: a fifty-fifty mixture of χ²(1) and χ²(2). Read the assumptions of any correction before you take its p-value.
- **Shrinkage, now for slopes.** A group's predicted slope is pulled hard towards the population slope when the group has few measurements or little spread in *x*; here groups keep about `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * std(mod) / std(ols)), "%")` of their own slope, and the spread of the predictions is not σ_1.
- **Conditional residuals, and the rows that set the scale.** `fitted` and `residuals` are population-level; subtract *both* of the group's own numbers, read the worm plot for shape and not for σ, name the rows far from their own group before standardising, and say what moves with them out — here ρ went to the edge of its range.
- **A random slope on an unsplit covariate does two jobs.** Its variance absorbs the between-versus-within contrast the fixed part refused to separate; on the blended column σ_1 would have been `{julia} round(sd1_blend, digits = 3)` rather than `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 3)`, and `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * (1 - stat / stat_blend)), "%")` of the likelihood-ratio evidence would have been misspecification — Bates et al. (2015) against Barr et al. (2013), in one file.

### Julia you used

- **`leftjoin(df, other, on = :BirdID)` and `indexin(a, b)`.** The join attaches the columns of `other` to every row of `df` whose key matches; `indexin` gives each element of `a` its position in `b`. The two lookups you no longer build by hand.
- **`nothing` as a cell's last line.** Stops the cell printing a value nobody needs to see.
- **`Dict{Symbol,Float64}()` and `d[k] = v`.** An empty lookup table with declared key and value types, filled one entry at a time.
- **`:y => (v -> cond ? a : missing) => :sw`.** An anonymous function inside `combine`, and `missing` as a value a later `skipmissing` steps over.
- **`V[1, 2]` and `B[:, 2]`.** Row one, column two of a matrix; the whole second column.
- **`return (; sd0 = s0, ...)` and `map(f, xs)`.** An explicit return of a NamedTuple, and a function applied to each element of a list with the results collected.
- **`findall(v)`, `setdiff(1:n, bad)`, `df[keep, :]`.** The positions where a true/false vector is true, one set of positions with another removed, and the rows at those positions.

### Calls you used

- `@formula(y ~ x + (1 + x|g))`: the random slope. Everything else about the call is unchanged from Class 6.
- `vc(fit)[:g]`: the 2 × 2 covariance of a correlated block; the diagonal's square roots are σ₀ and σ₁, the off-diagonal over their product is ρ. Why `re_sd` is empty here is in [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html).
- `ranef(fit)[:g]`: intercept deviations in column one, slope deviations in column two, in the order of `sort(unique(df.g))`.
- `aic(fit)`, `loglik(fit)`, `dof(fit)`, `lrtest(reduced, full)`: the comparison and the naive test, which warns when the extra parameters include a variance. The Stram and Lee mixture is one line: `0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(1), s) + 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(2), s)`.

## Further reading

*Graded by depth. Checked on 2026-09-07 against OpenAlex, an open catalogue of research papers.*

1. **Schielzeth, H. & Forstmeier, W. (2009) "Conclusions beyond support: overconfident estimates in mixed models", *Behavioral Ecology* 20:416–420.** doi:10.1093/beheco/arn145. Start here: leaving a random slope out of a repeated-measures model inflates confidence in the fixed effect. Short, concrete, and about animals.
2. **Barr, D. J., Levy, R., Scheepers, C. & Tily, H. J. (2013) "Random effects structure for confirmatory hypothesis testing: Keep it maximal", *Journal of Memory and Language* 68:255–278.** doi:10.1016/j.jml.2012.11.001. One half of the argument: fit the random-effects structure the design justifies, slopes included, or your fixed-effect test is anticonservative. Read with item 3 beside it.
3. **Bates, D., Kliegl, R., Vasishth, S. & Baayen, H. (2015) "Parsimonious mixed models", arXiv:1506.04967.** doi:10.48550/arxiv.1506.04967. The other half, and **not** the lme4 paper Class 8 will cite, despite the year and first author: maximal models are routinely over-parameterised. This chapter's example is the blended fit, where a random slope on the unsplit covariate carried a fixed effect nobody had specified. A preprint, widely cited, never in a journal.
4. **Matuschek, H., Kliegl, R., Vasishth, S., Baayen, H. & Bates, D. (2017) "Balancing Type I error and power in linear mixed models", *Journal of Memory and Language* 94:305–315.** doi:10.1016/j.jml.2017.01.001. The referee between items 2 and 3, with simulations.
5. **Stram, D. O. & Lee, J. W. (1994) "Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model", *Biometrics* 50:1171–1177**, doi:10.2307/2533455, **with its published correction, *Biometrics* (1995) 51:1196**, doi:10.2307/2533038. The direct source for the mixture used in class, stated for exactly this step: *q* random effects against *q* + 1. Read the correction as well as the paper; Self and Liang (1987), which Jaro named, is the theory underneath it.
6. **Gelman, A. & Hill, J. (2007) *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models*.** Chapters 12 and 13: varying slopes drawn six ways, and the within-versus-between decomposition at book length. Ignore the software.

```{julia}
# Exercises 1 to 4: sparrows.
ex_sp = dropmissing(sparrows, [:Tail])
ex_sp.Tail = Float64.(ex_sp.Tail)
ex_t_ri  = drm(bf(@formula(Tail ~ wc + (1|BirdID))),          Gaussian(); data = ex_sp)
ex_t_sep = drm(bf(@formula(Tail ~ wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = ex_sp)

ex_pool = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar)), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
ex_se_pool, ex_se_ri = stderror(ex_pool), stderror(sep_ri)

ex_rho_fit = Dict{Float64,Float64}()
for o in (-2.0, 2.0)
    d = DataFrame(BirdID = sparrows.BirdID, Wing = sparrows.Wing, wbar = sparrows.wbar,
                  x = sparrows.wdev .- o)
    f = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ x + wbar + (1 + x|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)
    W = vc(f)[:BirdID]
    ex_rho_fit[o] = W[1, 2] / sqrt(W[1, 1] * W[2, 2])
end

# Exercises 5 to 8: tadpoles.
ex_td = CSV.read("../data/ch8/tadpoles.csv", DataFrame)
ex_J = length(unique(ex_td.pond))
ex_pm = combine(groupby(ex_td, :pond), :days => mean => :m)
ex_joined = leftjoin(ex_td, ex_pm, on = :pond)
ex_td.dc = ex_td.days .- mean(ex_td.days)
ex_td.dmean = ex_joined.m .- mean(ex_td.days)
ex_td.ddev = ex_td.days .- ex_joined.m
ex_days_fit = drm(bf(@formula(days ~ 1 + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_days_within = 1 - repeatability(ex_days_fit).estimate
ex_ri = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ dc + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_sep = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ ddev + dmean + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_rs = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ dc + (1 + dc|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_V = vc(ex_rs)[:pond]
ex_sd1 = sqrt(ex_V[2, 2])
ex_rho = ex_V[1, 2] / (sqrt(ex_V[1, 1]) * ex_sd1)
ex_stat = 2 * (loglik(ex_rs) - loglik(ex_ri))
ex_p_naive = lrtest(ex_ri, ex_rs).pvalue
ex_p_mix = p_sl(ex_stat)
ex_B = ranef(ex_rs)[:pond]
ex_groups = sort(unique(ex_td.pond))
ex_model_slope = coef(ex_rs, :mu)[2] .+ ex_B[:, 2]
ex_own_slope = zeros(ex_J)
for (i, g) in enumerate(ex_groups)
    m = ex_td.pond .== g
    ex_own_slope[i] = cov(ex_td.dc[m], ex_td.length[m]) / var(ex_td.dc[m])
end
ex_spread_ratio = std(ex_model_slope) / std(ex_own_slope)
```

Graded by depth: the first three take ten minutes each. Exercises 1 to 4 run on the sparrow file the setup cell wrote, `data/ch7/sparrows-weight.csv`, which carries `wc`, `wbar` and `wdev` already, so the take-home — split first, then free — is practised on real repeated measures. Exercises 5 to 8 run on Momo's tadpole file, `data/ch8/tadpoles.csv`, which Class 8 simulates from a stated seed: `{julia} nrow(ex_td)` tadpoles in `{julia} ex_J` ponds, each with its `days` since hatching and its body `length`. Know what that file can and cannot show. It was drawn with one slope for every pond and ages drawn without regard to pond, so the split has nothing to find (it costs `{julia} round(aic(ex_sep) - aic(ex_ri), digits = 2)` of AIC) and the true σ₁ is zero. What it *can* show is what a random-slope fit, a boundary test and a caterpillar plot do when nobody has their own slope, the case you must be able to recognise. Do every exercise on your own organism as well. A *check* is a number computed from the named file when this page was built. **For every question, paste your code and then explain in your own words what each line does**, as if to somebody who has done Class 6 and not Class 7.

1. **Within and between, in the right order.** The chapter split mass for wing; do it for **tail**. Drop the rows with no tail, then fit `Tail ~ wdev + wbar + (1 | BirdID)` against `Tail ~ wc + (1 | BirdID)`. Report the two fixed slopes with their standard errors and both AICs. Two sentences: which slope the unsplit coefficient was closer to, and how much AIC the one extra fixed parameter bought. *Check:* within-bird slope `{julia} round(coef(ex_t_sep, :mu)[2], digits = 3)`, between-bird slope `{julia} round(coef(ex_t_sep, :mu)[3], digits = 3)`, unsplit `{julia} round(coef(ex_t_ri, :mu)[2], digits = 3)`; the split buys `{julia} round(aic(ex_t_ri) - aic(ex_t_sep), digits = 2)` of AIC.

2. **Both mechanisms on one screen.** Fit `Wing ~ wdev + wbar` with no bird term, then with `(1 | BirdID)`, and put the two standard errors of `wdev` and the two of `wbar` side by side. Before you look, predict which goes up and which goes down when the bird term arrives; then say which mechanism from class won for each column, and why the two columns pulled in opposite directions. *Check:* the standard error of `wbar` goes from `{julia} round(ex_se_pool[3], digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(ex_se_ri[3], digits = 4)`, and of `wdev` from `{julia} round(ex_se_pool[2], digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(ex_se_ri[2], digits = 4)`.

3. **The origin you report at.** Refit the chapter's random-slope model with `wdev` shifted two grams down and two grams up, inside the shaded strip. Report σ₁, ρ and the AIC of each, then get the same two correlations from the fitted Σ with the shift on the board, without refitting. One sentence: which origin you would report ρ at in a paper, and why. *Check:* ρ is `{julia} round(ex_rho_fit[-2.0], digits = 3)` two grams below and `{julia} round(ex_rho_fit[2.0], digits = 3)` two grams above, from the fit and from the formula alike, and σ₁ and the AIC do not move.

4. **The rows the fit was leaning on.** Refit the chapter's separated random-slope model and its random-intercept twin without the `{julia} length(bad)` rows the class named, and report σ, σ₁, ρ, the within-bird slope and the AIC the random slope buys, beside the full-file values. One number lands on the edge of the values it may take: say which, and what a Σ with that value says about how many separate things the birds are doing. Then write the one sentence you would put in a paper about these rows. *Check:* with the rows out, σ is `{julia} round(first(sigma(keep_rs)), digits = 3)`, ρ is `{julia} round(rho3, digits = 2)` and AIC prefers the random slope by `{julia} round(aic(keep_ri) - aic(keep_rs), digits = 2)`.

5. **Check before you fit.** Compute one minus the repeatability of `days`, the share of its variation within ponds, as the chapter's table did. One sentence: is `days` a thing that happened to each tadpole or to each pond, and why does that decide whether a random slope on it is a question with an answer? *Check:* the within share is `{julia} round(ex_days_within, digits = 2)`.

6. **Both fits, one term, when the truth is zero.** Fit `length ~ dc + (1 | pond)` and then `(1 + dc | pond)`. Report both fixed slopes, both standard errors, and the covariance block from `vc`. Then say what σ₁ came out as, what Class 8's cell says it should be, and why a fitted σ₁ is never exactly its true value. *Check:* σ₁ = `{julia} round(ex_sd1, digits = 3)` and ρ = `{julia} round(ex_rho, digits = 2)`; the standard error moves from `{julia} round(stderror(ex_ri)[2], digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(stderror(ex_rs)[2], digits = 4)`.

7. **The right mixture, at the null.** Compare the two fits of question 6 with `lrtest`, then with the Stram and Lee mixture computed by hand as the chapter did. Report both p-values, say which you would report and why **without** using the word "conservative" on its own — say what it is conservative *about* — and whether either would have led you to claim a spread of slopes the file does not have. *Check:* naive p = `{julia} round(ex_p_naive, digits = 2)`, mixture p = `{julia} round(ex_p_mix, digits = 2)`.

8. **The caterpillar, for slopes, when nobody has one.** Compute each pond's own least-squares slope from its points alone, and plot them against the model's slopes as the chapter's figure did. Report the ratio of the two spreads against the chapter's `{julia} round(std(mod) / std(ols), digits = 2)`. Two sentences: no pond really has its own slope, yet the ponds keep more of their own spread than the birds did — which fact about a pond, how many tadpoles or how well spread their ages, explains that; and why are the diamonds still not all on one line? *Check:* the model's slopes have `{julia} round(ex_spread_ratio, digits = 2)` of the spread of the ponds' own slopes.
